question: ultimate-reality
lede: God alone exists from himself. Everything else exists because the triune God freely made it and keeps it in being, so the world is real but never independent of its Creator.
scope: Reformed doctrine of God and creation: Scripture first, explained by Augustine, Calvin, Turretin and Bavinck and summarized in the Westminster Standards

question: something-rather-than-nothing
lede: God did not need a world. There is something rather than nothing because God freely chose to create it from nothing, and God himself needs no further explanation, because he exists from himself.
scope: Reformed doctrine of creation: Scripture first, explained by Augustine, Turretin and Bavinck and summarized in the Westminster Standards

question: ultimate-personal
lede: Yes. The ultimate reality is a God who knows, wills, loves and speaks, and he is personal in himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, not only in his dealings with the world.
scope: Reformed doctrine of God's personal attributes and the Trinity: Scripture first, explained by Augustine, Calvin, Turretin and Bavinck and summarized in the Westminster Standards

question: order
lede: Reality is orderly because one wise God made it by wisdom and faithfully governs it. The regularities we call laws of nature are his steady ordinances, working through real created causes.
scope: Reformed doctrine of creation by wisdom and providence through second causes: Scripture first, explained by Augustine, Calvin, Turretin and Bavinck and summarized in the Westminster Standards

question: one-and-many
lede: God is one being in three persons, so unity and distinction are both basic in him. The created world's real unity and real variety reflect that, faintly, as the work of one wise Creator.
scope: Reformed doctrine of the Trinity and of creation's unity-in-diversity, as Scripture states it and Bavinck explains it, with Van Til's apologetic development
provenanceNotes: bavinck-reformed-dogmatics-monergism-2 Vol. 2, §27.25, PDF pp. 385–387: automated English translation; paraphrased

question: knowledge-possible
lede: Human beings can know reality because God made both the world and the minds that encounter it. Our knowledge is real but finite, and sin distorts how we use it without making knowledge impossible.
scope: Reformed doctrine of human knowledge: Scripture first, explained by Augustine, Calvin, Turretin and Bavinck, restated apologetically by Van Til, and summarized in the Westminster Standards
provenanceNotes: sep-epistemology-naturalized §2: Quine 1969c, p. 126, as quoted by SEP

question: logic-binding
lede: Logic binds every mind because the one wise God made both the world and the minds that reason about it. Its laws are discovered, not invented, and they hold of things, not merely of our thoughts.
scope: Reformed account of logic: Scripture's use of reasoning, Augustine's realism about valid inference, Turretin and Bavinck on God-given laws of thought, and Van Til's later apologetic claim, distinguished from the older doctrine
provenanceNotes: bavinck-reformed-dogmatics-monergism-1 Vol. 1, §7, PDF p. 217: automated English translation; paraphrased

van-til-defense p. 297: quoting Van Til's Introduction to Theology syllabus

question: induction
lede: Christians expect nature's patterns to continue because a faithful God established its ordinary order and sustains it. That gives a reason to expect regularity; it is not a proof that escapes Hume's circle.
scope: Reformed doctrine of providence as the ground of expected regularity: Scripture, Augustine and the Westminster Confession, with Van Til's later transcendental claim distinguished from the doctrine

question: ultimate-authority
lede: God is the final authority, and his written Word is the supreme rule by which every human authority, tradition and argument is judged. Reason and the church serve that Word; they do not sit above it.
scope: Reformed doctrine of Scripture's authority: Scripture first, including Christ's own reception of it, explained by Calvin, Turretin and Bavinck, with Van Til's apologetic development, and summarized in the Westminster Confession and the Belgic Confession
provenanceNotes: bavinck-reformed-dogmatics-monergism-1 Vol. 1, §11.10, PDF pp. 412–414: automated English translation; paraphrased
turretin-institutio-1847 I.10.1–3: Latin (organice et ministerialiter, non despotice); our translation
sep-quine §3.3: Quine 1951, as quoted by SEP

question: what-is-man
lede: Man is a creature of dust and divine breath, one person of body and soul, made male and female as God's image; fallen, he remains that image.
scope: Reformed anthropology: Scripture first, expounded by Calvin, Turretin and Bavinck and summarized in the Westminster Standards
provenanceNotes: bavinck-reformed-dogmatics-monergism-2 Vol. 2, §33.8, 33.10, PDF pp. 659, 669–671: automated English translation; paraphrased

question: why-alive
lede: Humans are alive because God made them for himself, to glorify and enjoy him forever, receiving ordinary life from him and returning it to him.
scope: Reformed teaching on the chief end of man: Scripture, Augustine and Edwards, summarized in the Westminster Standards

question: offspring-family
lede: Marriage and procreation are creation ordinances, blessed before the Fall; the household passes on covenant faith, and singleness can be a gift.
scope: Reformed teaching on marriage, children and household: Scripture, Calvin and Bavinck, with Westminster

question: love-beauty-creativity
lede: Humans love, seek beauty and make things because they image a God who is love, whose glory is beautiful; these gifts are good when ordered to him.
scope: Reformed teaching on love, beauty and the arts: Scripture, Augustine, Calvin and Edwards, with Heidelberg's limits on images

question: worship
lede: Humans worship because they were made to know and serve God; idolatry is that religious nature turned to created things, and worship belongs to God alone.
scope: Reformed teaching on religion, worship and idolatry: Scripture, Calvin, Bavinck and Turretin, with Westminster and Heidelberg

question: great-and-terrible
lede: Man is great because he remains God's image-bearer, and terrible because that one created nature is corrupted at the root of the will, yet restrained and gifted by God.
scope: Reformed anthropology: the biblical history of creation, fall and preservation, expounded by Augustine, Calvin and Edwards within the Westminster Standards

question: know-the-good
lede: Moral awareness is a real but damaged knowledge of God’s law: conscience survives the Fall, while Scripture corrects its partial and self-serving judgments.
scope: Scripture on conscience and the law written on the heart, expounded by Calvin and Turretin on natural law, with the Westminster Standards and the Canons of Dort

question: fail-the-good
lede: We can recognize moral truth while loving what opposes it: sin disorders the will, and even renewed believers must struggle against its remaining power.
scope: Scripture and the Westminster Standards, with Calvin and Edwards on moral knowledge and inability

question: evil
lede: At root, evil is sin, culpable departure from God's law, and it corrupts the good gifts God created. God governs even evil, as at the cross, without being its author, and Christ will finally defeat it.
scope: Confessional Reformed evil, privation, providence and the evidential objection

question: suffering
lede: Suffering belongs to a world disordered by sin yet governed by God. The Son entered it and suffered for sinners, so believers' afflictions can become discipline rather than condemnation, though their particular purposes often stay hidden.
scope: Scripture’s fallen creation, Reformed providence, and the distinction between general sin and personal blame

question: death
lede: Death is a judgment within humanity’s fallen condition and an enemy; for believers its sting is removed, without making bodily death itself good.
scope: Reformed account of death’s cause, wrongness and altered significance

question: self-deception
lede: We can resist truths we recognize because sinful love redirects attention, interpretation, and self-examination toward protecting what we want.
scope: Scripture, Westminster, and Augustine on recognized truth resisted by disordered love

question: self-salvation
lede: Man’s problem is guilt and corruption before God; Christ reconciles and renews his people through grace, producing real faith, repentance and obedience rather than self-earned rescue.
scope: Confessional Reformed diagnosis, Christ’s work and its application

question: guilt
lede: God forgives real guilt without setting justice aside. Christ bore the judgment sinners deserve and gives his righteousness to all who trust him; repentance and repair follow, but never buy pardon.
scope: Christ's atoning work, justification by faith, conscience and repair in Reformed teaching

question: after-death
lede: Death separates body and soul; believers are with Christ while awaiting the resurrection of the same embodied person and the final judgment.
scope: Confessional Reformed intermediate state, resurrection and judgment

question: final-end
lede: The final good is holy, embodied communion with God in Christ, shared with his people in renewed creation; everlasting judgment is also part of the claim.
scope: Reformed glorification, communion and the renewed creation

question: revelation
lede: Yes. God shows himself in the world he made, and he has spoken and acted in history, above all in Jesus Christ, whom Scripture records and interprets. Its central claim, the resurrection, is a public event open to testing.
scope: Reformed doctrine of general and special revelation: Scripture first, with Augustine, Calvin and Bavinck on how revelation is recognized, and the Westminster and Belgic Confessions as synthesis; the historical case for the resurrection is examined under the Jesus question

question: history
lede: History is linear and going somewhere. It has a real beginning in creation, a centre in Christ's death and resurrection, and a real end in judgement and new creation, and God's providence directs it throughout.
scope: Reformed theology of history: the biblical arc from creation to new creation, Augustine's two cities and his rejection of cycles, Bavinck on Christ's rule and the renewal of creation, and the Westminster Confession on the one covenant and the day of judgement

question: jesus
lede: Jesus is the eternal Son of God made man, the promised Messiah, who was crucified for sinners, raised bodily from the dead and exalted as Lord, and who will return to judge and renew the world.
scope: Reformed Christology from Scripture (John 1, Colossians 2, Romans 1, 1 Corinthians 15), Calvin and the Westminster Confession, with the historical case argued from the shared evidence base (Paul, the Gospels, Josephus, Tacitus) and the critical scholarship of Martin, Ehrman and Lowder alongside Craig, Habermas and Hurtado

question: ultimate-reality
lede: Nature is all there is: no God or supernatural order stands behind it. Most naturalists hold that everything is physical or built from the physical, though they still debate minds, numbers and laws.
scope: Ontological naturalism as held by contemporary philosophers and scientists, with Hume and Russell as founding modern voices; physicalism treated as the majority view, not the definition

question: something-rather-than-nothing
lede: Naturalists do not claim that something came from nothing. Most hold that reality, or its basic laws and state, may simply exist without a deeper reason, or doubt that 'nothing' was ever a real alternative.
scope: Naturalist responses to the existence question: Hume's Dialogues, Russell's reply as reported in the literature, and Sean Carroll's contemporary treatment

question: ultimate-personal
lede: Naturalism finds no good reason to think a mind or person underlies nature. Minds appeared late and locally in cosmic history, as products of natural processes rather than their source.
scope: Naturalist reasons for not positing a personal ground of nature (Russell; Carroll), with physicalist, emergentist and panpsychist variants

question: order
lede: Nature's regularities are a basic feature of the world, not the work of a designer. Naturalists disagree about what laws are, summaries of what happens or real necessities in nature, but agree that no designer is needed.
scope: Naturalist accounts of regularity and laws (Humean, non-Humean, antirealist), Hume's critique of causation and design, and responses to cosmic fine-tuning

question: one-and-many
lede: Naturalism has no special doctrine of the one and the many. Its answer is that reality is one natural, causally connected world, organized into many real levels and things.
scope: Physicalism, emergence and composition as naturalist resources for unity and plurality; not a native naturalist doctrine

question: knowledge-possible
lede: Human cognition is part of nature. Perception, memory and reasoning are evolved capacities, reliable enough to live by and continually corrected through experience, criticism and scientific inquiry.
scope: Naturalized epistemology (Quine, as presented in SEP) and its moderate successors, Hume's account of belief, scientific realism and its critics, and the debate over evolution and the reliability of cognition
provenanceNotes: sep-epistemology-naturalized §2: Quine 1969c, p. 126, as quoted by SEP
sep-epistemology-naturalized §2: Quine 1969b, p. 82, as quoted by SEP

question: logic-binding
lede: Naturalists agree that logic binds but disagree about why: because it states basic facts about the world, because it is built into our language or cognition, or because it is our most deeply entrenched belief.
scope: Naturalist options on the status of logic: Russell's realism, conventionalism and Quine's regress objection, Quinean revisability, and recent a posteriori accounts (Maddy, Azzouni, Sher), as mapped by SEP
provenanceNotes: sep-quine §3.3: Quine 1951, as quoted by SEP

question: induction
lede: Induction works because nature is in fact regular, but naturalists disagree on how to justify expecting that: some accept a benign circle, some infer real laws, and some say induction is simply what reasonableness means.
scope: Hume's problem of induction at full strength (Enquiry IV–V, Treatise 1.3.6; Russell's restatement) and the main naturalist responses as mapped by SEP: circular-but-benign, explanatory, probabilistic, dissolving and pragmatic answers, and Hume's own scepticism
provenanceNotes: sep-epistemology-naturalized §2: Quine 1969c, as quoted by SEP

question: ultimate-authority
lede: Claims answer finally to a revisable network of observation, reasoning, coherence, predictive success and public inquiry. Naturalism has no final text or institution, and it places no belief beyond revision.
scope: Methodological naturalism: Quine's holism and rejection of first philosophy (as presented in SEP), Hume's mitigated scepticism, and the debate over the circularity of naturalized epistemology
provenanceNotes: sep-quine §§3.2–3.3: Quine 1951, as quoted by SEP
sep-epistemology-naturalized §3.1: Fumerton 1994, as quoted by SEP

question: what-is-man
lede: A human being is an evolved social animal whose mind and self are realized in a living body and brain; naturalists differ over how persons persist.
scope: Mainstream evolutionary naturalism from Darwin and Russell to contemporary philosophy of mind and personal identity; reductive and nonreductive variants

question: why-alive
lede: No cosmic purpose explains human existence; meaning is conferred by what people care about or found in objectively valuable goods such as love and knowledge.
scope: Naturalistic humanism from Russell to contemporary debates over meaning: subjectivist, objectivist and nihilist positions

question: offspring-family
lede: Reproduction and family are products of evolution, from sexual selection to kin-directed care; their origin explains them without settling how families ought to be.
scope: Evolutionary and Humean accounts of sex, kinship and family, kept separate from humanist ethical argument

question: love-beauty-creativity
lede: Love, the sense of beauty and creativity are evolved capacities shaped by culture; their origin does not make them illusions, and no single theory is settled.
scope: Hume and Darwin as founding naturalist accounts of love, beauty and art; no single contemporary theory assumed

question: worship
lede: Religious devotion is a natural product of human cognition and emotion; its naturalness neither proves nor disproves religion, and humanists may revere human ideals instead.
scope: Naturalistic accounts of religion from Hume and Darwin to the cognitive science of religion, with Russell's humanist reverence

question: great-and-terrible
lede: The same evolved social and cognitive capacities that make conscience, cooperation and culture possible can also be recruited for partiality, deception, dominance and organized violence.
scope: Mainstream evolutionary naturalism from Hume and Darwin to contemporary moral psychology; realist and anti-realist metaethics

question: know-the-good
lede: People learn right from wrong through evolved social feelings like sympathy, corrected by reflection, experience and a more impartial view. Realists hold that this can track objective moral facts; anti-realists, that it projects values.
scope: Darwin and Hume on moral cognition, Railton’s realism, and Mackie’s error theory

question: fail-the-good
lede: Moral judgment is one influence among competing motives: immediate desire can override reflective concern, while lasting social feelings return afterward as remorse.
scope: Humean and Darwinian moral psychology, with naturalistic moral realism distinguished from explanations of motivation

question: evil
lede: Evil names the gravest harms people inflict, explained by natural motives such as limited sympathy, competition for scarce goods and aggression, not by a supernatural power; naturalists differ over whether its wrongness is objective.
scope: Naturalist causal explanation, rival moral theories and the concept of evil

question: suffering
lede: Suffering is what vulnerable, sentient creatures undergo through injury, disease, aging and harm done by others. It has natural causes to understand and relieve, but no providential purpose behind it.
scope: Hume’s account of natural vulnerability, existing aging science, and Russell’s human remedies

question: death
lede: Death ends a person’s life through natural processes; its badness is disputed, especially between the absence of later experience and the loss of possible goods.
scope: Natural mortality and competing philosophical evaluations of death

question: self-deception
lede: Desire, fear, and self-interest can bias how evidence is selected and interpreted, producing mistaken confidence without a deliberate plan to lie to oneself.
scope: Motivated belief accounts, with Russell on rationalized cruelty

question: self-salvation
lede: Naturalistic humanism seeks fallible personal and social improvement through knowledge, care and cooperation, with no supernatural salvation or guarantee that every loss will be repaired.
scope: Representative naturalistic humanism rather than a religious salvation scheme

question: guilt
lede: Real wrongdoing calls for acknowledgment, accountability and repair; interpersonal forgiveness can change a relationship without making the past innocent.
scope: Secular moral responsibility and interpersonal forgiveness

question: after-death
lede: On the ordinary naturalist view, death ends the person: when the living body stops, no one remains to think or feel. Theories of personal identity differ, but neither bodily nor psychological accounts establish an afterlife.
scope: Russell’s mortalism with philosophical distinctions about persistence

question: final-end
lede: Naturalistic humanism seeks finite flourishing, knowledge and humane relationships; it offers no guaranteed personal or cosmic final state.
scope: Representative naturalistic humanist goods and limits of progress

question: revelation
lede: Naturalism finds no good evidence that any god has revealed itself. It treats revelation claims as human testimony, and because experience strongly favours natural causes, such claims need unusually strong evidence.
scope: Naturalistic assessment of revelation claims as testimony: Hume's 'Of Miracles', the post-Humean debate over priors and evidence (as mapped in SEP), and religious diversity and natural explanation as defeaters of religious experience

question: history
lede: Nature gives history no built-in purpose or final goal. Time has a physical direction and life has evolved, but any progress is made by human beings toward goals they value, and nothing guarantees it will last.
scope: Naturalistic views of history as a whole: the physical arrow of time without purpose, evolution without a goal, contingent moral and social progress (Darwin, Railton, the Humanist Manifesto) and the absence of any final consummation (Russell)

question: jesus
lede: Jesus was a real first-century Jewish prophet who was crucified, and his followers very early came to believe he had risen. Naturalism explains that belief through visions, interpretation and legend, without a resurrection.
scope: Critical-historical naturalism on Jesus: the facts critical historians grant and dispute (Martin, Ehrman, Lowder), the best natural explanation of resurrection belief (visions, scriptural interpretation, legendary growth), and the metaphysical prior against miracle (Hume; the historian's limit as Ehrman states it)

question: ultimate-reality
lede: There is one God, the Creator, and the world he made. God depends on nothing, everything else depends wholly on him, and nothing in creation shares his kind of existence.
scope: Tanakh and rabbinic tradition, systematized by the medieval philosophers (Saadia, Maimonides) with Halevi as the covenantal counterweight

question: something-rather-than-nothing
lede: The world exists because God willed it into being. The main line of rabbinic and medieval thought holds that he created it from nothing, with no eternal material beside him.
scope: Genesis and rabbinic tradition, with the medieval arguments of Saadia, Maimonides, Halevi and Nachmanides

question: ultimate-personal
lede: Yes. The God of the Torah speaks, commands, loves and judges, and is addressed in prayer. Jewish philosophers disagree over how far that personal language describes God himself rather than his actions.
scope: Tanakh and rabbinic piety, with the philosophical debate between Maimonides (with Saadia) and Halevi

question: order
lede: The world is orderly because God made it with wisdom and set fixed laws for heaven and earth. Jewish thinkers disagree over how much of life runs by that natural order and how much by God's hidden, direct care.
scope: Tanakh and Midrash on wisdom and the laws of heaven and earth, with the debate between Maimonides and Nachmanides on nature and providence

question: one-and-many
lede: God alone is truly one, with a unity unlike anything in the world. The many belong to creation, which God made as one ordered whole, so plurality is real but always created and dependent.
scope: Maimonides on divine unity and the unity of the created world, with Ḥabad Ḥasidism as a material variant; there is no single rabbinic doctrine of the one and the many

question: knowledge-possible
lede: People can know the world because God made them with senses and reason that genuinely work. Wisdom is God's gift, reliable testimony carries knowledge between generations, and some things remain beyond human reach.
scope: The Hebrew Bible's wisdom tradition, with the medieval accounts of Saadia Gaon (roots of knowledge), Judah Halevi (historical testimony) and Maimonides (demonstration and its limits)

question: logic-binding
lede: Rabbinic tradition reasons rigorously but has no doctrine of why logic binds. Its philosophers held that the impossible stays impossible even for God, because it is nothing at all, not a limit on his power.
scope: Rabbinic tradition has no doctrine of the ground of logic; the answer draws on the medieval philosophers Saadia Gaon and Maimonides on the impossible and on how the intellect knows it
provenanceNotes: saadia-emunot-ibn-tibbon II.13: Hebrew; our translation of the phrases

question: induction
lede: Jewish tradition expects the world to keep its course because God established fixed laws for heaven and earth. That is a theological ground for expecting regularity; classical Jewish sources do not take up Hume's problem itself.
scope: The Hebrew Bible's fixed laws of heaven and earth, the Talmud's 'the world follows its course', and Maimonides' defence of stable natures against the kalam; classical Jewish sources do not address Hume's problem

question: ultimate-authority
lede: Final authority belongs to God's revelation at Sinai: the Written Torah and the Oral Torah given with it, as interpreted by the authorized sages. Reason serves the interpretation of that revelation rather than rivalling it.
scope: Rabbinic authority from Sinai through the Written and Oral Torah and the authorized court (Deuteronomy 17, Avot 1:1, Bava Metzia 59b), with Saadia, Halevi, Maimonides and Nachmanides on reason, prophecy and interpretation
provenanceNotes: saadia-emunot-ibn-tibbon III.8: Hebrew; our translation of the phrase

question: what-is-man
lede: The human being is earth and divine breath, made in God's image as male and female, unique and free, joining earthly and heavenly traits in one life.
scope: Tanakh and classical rabbinic texts, with Saadia and Maimonides as philosophical interpreters

question: why-alive
lede: Humans are created to serve God through Torah, worship and kindness, doing every ordinary deed for the sake of heaven; Maimonides adds knowledge of God.
scope: Tanakh and classical rabbinic sources, with Maimonides' intellectualist account as one major strand

question: offspring-family
lede: Procreation is a commandment rooted in creation, marriage is joy and blessing, and the home passes on the covenant, though the sages record disputes and an exception.
scope: Tanakh, Mishnah and Talmud on procreation and marriage, with Maimonides; modern streams noted, not adjudicated

question: love-beauty-creativity
lede: Love of God and neighbour is commanded, beauty is blessed and offered back to God in beautified commandments, and creativity answers a divine mandate.
scope: Tanakh and rabbinic texts on love, beauty and craft, with Maimonides and Soloveitchik; attitudes to figurative art not generalized

question: worship
lede: Worship belongs to the one God alone; after the Temple it is above all prayer, the service of the heart, and idolatry begins as misdirected honour.
scope: Tanakh and rabbinic sources on avodah and idolatry, with Maimonides' account of idolatry's origin

question: great-and-terrible
lede: Each person bears God's image and a created inclination that both builds the world and pulls toward sin; free and responsible, he is to govern it through Torah and repentance.
scope: Classical rabbinic texts, with medieval philosophical and Hasidic readings

question: know-the-good
lede: A person knows the good through Torah, which is near, to be understood and done, and through reason, which can grasp duties such as gratitude and avoiding harm; some commandments are known only because God gave them.
scope: Tanakh, rabbinic moral reasoning and Noahide duties, with Saadia and Maimonides

question: fail-the-good
lede: A person can intend to obey God while an opposing inclination gains strength through habit; Torah, divine help, and disciplined choice address that struggle.
scope: Tanakh and classical rabbinic teaching on inclination, Torah and choice, with Maimonides on character

question: evil
lede: Moral evil is a person's own wrongdoing: the inclination, good in its place, grows into a master when indulged and is governed through Torah and God's help. Calamity comes under the one Creator's rule, not a rival power.
scope: Biblical creation, rabbinic inclination and Maimonidean evil

question: suffering
lede: Jewish sources offer several accounts of suffering—retribution, loving discipline, human wrongdoing, and acknowledged mystery—without authorizing one explanation for every sufferer.
scope: Job and the plural rabbinic accounts of affliction, with Maimonides’ interpretation

question: death
lede: Death is the appointed limit of a finite life, calling for wisdom, repentance and accountability before God. The sages differ over its tie to sin, and the tradition awaits the resurrection of the dead.
scope: Biblical mortality and a deliberately plural rabbinic account

question: self-deception
lede: The inclination can make repeated wrongdoing seem permissible and turn self-approval into rationalization; reflection before God interrupts that process.
scope: Tanakh and rabbinic accounts of self-approval, repeated sin, and moral self-examination

question: self-salvation
lede: Sin and disordered inclination call for covenantal return: Torah, teshuvah, changed conduct and God’s mercy restore nearness, with divine help and the World to Come within the hope.
scope: Rabbinic covenantal repentance with Maimonides and Nachmanides

question: guilt
lede: Teshuvah joins confession and changed conduct with divine mercy; Yom Kippur does not bypass reconciliation for wrongs against another person.
scope: Tanakh and rabbinic repentance, with Maimonides

question: after-death
lede: After death each person faces God's judgment, and the dead will be raised; the Mishnah excludes from the World to Come anyone who denies that resurrection is taught in the Torah. How resurrection, the soul and that World relate is disputed.
scope: Biblical/rabbinic resurrection with Maimonides’ distinct reward account

question: final-end
lede: The final good is life with God in the World to Come. Maimonides, a major but not the only voice, describes it as incorporeal delight in knowing God, beyond the messianic age of peace that serves it.
scope: Rabbinic final good with Maimonides and a contrasting heart-restoration strand

question: revelation
lede: Yes. God revealed himself publicly to the whole people of Israel at Mount Sinai, and the Torah has been handed down from that event. Its warrant is the shared witness of an entire nation, not one prophet's wonders.
scope: Rabbinic Judaism on revelation: the public revelation at Sinai (Exodus 19–20, Deuteronomy 5) and the tests for later prophets (Deuteronomy 13, 18), as argued by Maimonides, Halevi and Saadia, with the modern Kuzari principle and critical scholarship on the exodus for historical evaluation

question: history
lede: History is linear and covenantal, moving from creation through exile toward redemption. God will restore Israel under a messianic king, and beyond that lie the resurrection of the dead and the World to Come.
scope: Rabbinic view of history as covenantal and linear: exile and redemption, Maimonides' this-worldly messianic age (Laws of Kings 11–12), the resurrection and the World to Come kept distinct (Laws of Repentance 9), with Saadia on the certainty of redemption and Talmudic messianic chronologies
provenanceNotes: saadia-emunot-ibn-tibbon VIII.1; VIII.8: Hebrew; our paraphrase

question: jesus
lede: Jesus is not the Messiah and is not divine. The redemption the prophets promised has not come, and the unity of God rules out any incarnation.
scope: Rabbinic and medieval Jewish judgements on Jesus: Maimonides' messianic criteria and his uncensored account of Jesus (Laws of Kings 11), Nachmanides at the Barcelona disputation, Saadia on Daniel 9, with the Talmud's later Jesus passage assessed as legend rather than first-century evidence
provenanceNotes: nachmanides-vikuach-wikisource second day: Hebrew; our paraphrase
nachmanides-vikuach-wikisource first and second days: Hebrew; our paraphrase

question: ultimate-reality
lede: God alone is uncreated, self-sufficient and beyond comparison. Everything else is his creation, brought into being by his command and dependent on him at every moment.
scope: Qur'an and Sunni theology (Ash'ari and Maturidi kalām, Ibn Taymiyya), with Ibn Sina's philosophy as the major alternative they answered

question: something-rather-than-nothing
lede: The world exists because God willed it and said 'Be.' Muslim thinkers agree on that dependence but disagree about its timeline: a world with a first moment, an eternal emanation, or God creating without beginning.
scope: Qur'an and hadith, with the three classical answers: kalām (Ash'ari, Maturidi, al-Ghazali), Ibn Sina's philosophy, and Ibn Taymiyya

question: ultimate-personal
lede: Yes. God is the Ever-Living who knows, hears, sees, wills, speaks and shows mercy. Yet 'there is nothing like Him,' so his personal life is affirmed without picturing him in human terms.
scope: Qur'an and Sunni creed (al-Ash'ari), with the Mu'tazili and philosophical alternatives and Ibn Taymiyya

question: order
lede: The world is orderly because God creates all things in due measure and his way does not change. Muslim thinkers disagree about whether created things have real causal powers or God directly creates each event by his custom.
scope: Qur'an on measure and God's unchanging practice, with the classical dispute over causation: Ash'ari occasionalism (al-Ghazali), Maturidi natures, Ibn Taymiyya's secondary causes and Ibn Rushd's natural causation

question: one-and-many
lede: God is absolutely one, without partner or rival. The many are his creatures, each a sign of his one wisdom and each praising him, so plurality is real but always created and dependent.
scope: Qur'anic tawḥīd and created plurality, the Sunni doctrine of attributes, and Ibn 'Arabi's contested monism

question: knowledge-possible
lede: People can know because God gave them senses, reason and an inborn disposition toward truth, and filled the world with signs. Knowledge comes through perception, reliable report and reasoning; revelation completes it.
scope: The Qur'an on human faculties and signs; the Sunni creed of al-Nasafi (Maturidi); al-Ghazali's crisis of certainty; Ibn Taymiyya on the natural disposition (fitra), from SEP and his al-Radd ʿalā al-manṭiqiyyīn

question: logic-binding
lede: Islamic thought treats the basic laws of reasoning as immediate knowledge that God built into every sound mind. Its scholars all accepted valid inference but disagreed over whether Aristotelian logic deserves special authority.
scope: Sunni accounts of necessary rational knowledge (al-Nasafi's creed; al-Juwayni via SEP; Ibn Taymiyya via SEP and his al-Radd ʿalā al-manṭiqiyyīn), and the contrast between al-Ghazali's acceptance of Aristotelian logic and Ibn Taymiyya's critique
provenanceNotes: sep-al-ghazali §7.3: al-Juwayni, as quoted by SEP
ibn-taymiyya-radd-mantiqiyyin pp. 250–251, 293, 296–297: Arabic checked; quotations in SEP's translation

question: induction
lede: Muslim theologians expect nature's patterns to continue because God keeps a constant custom in creating. They disagreed over whether created causes have real powers of their own or merely accompany what God creates.
scope: Al-Ghazali on causation and God's unchanging custom (Tahafut 17 and Ihya' 31, via SEP and the Bouyges Arabic); created causal powers in Ibn Taymiyya and the Maturidis; Ibn Taymiyya's empiricism (al-Radd ʿalā al-manṭiqiyyīn and SEP); Ibn Rushd's necessitarian reply
provenanceNotes: averroes-tahafut-bouyges Phys. Disc. I, pp. 517–518: Arabic; paraphrased
averroes-tahafut-bouyges Phys. Disc. I, p. 519: Arabic; paraphrased
ibn-taymiyya-radd-mantiqiyyin p. 300: Arabic; paraphrased, with the quoted sentence in our translation

question: ultimate-authority
lede: The Qur'an and the authentic Sunna of the Prophet are the final authorities. Reason recognizes that revelation is genuine and helps interpret it, and the scholars' consensus and methods extend it to new cases.
scope: Sunni authority: the Qur'an and Sunna; al-Shafi'i's Risāla on the Sunna, consensus and analogy, with Macdonald's (1903) account of the later four-source scheme; al-Nasafi's creed on prophetic report; al-Ghazali's rule of interpretation and Ibn Taymiyya's no-conflict thesis (Darʾ taʿāruḍ); the Twelver Shi'a Imamate in al-Saduq's creed
provenanceNotes: shafii-risala-shakir §§1321–1334, pp. 476–479: Arabic; paraphrased, with the quoted phrase in our translation

question: what-is-man
lede: The human being is clay given life by God's breathed spirit, honoured and born on the fitra; the real self is the heart, accountable to God.
scope: The Qur'an and sound hadith, with al-Ghazali's psychology of the heart and the Sunni theological schools

question: why-alive
lede: God created humans to worship Him, needing nothing from them; life is a test, and al-Ghazali makes love of God its final aim.
scope: The Qur'an and sound hadith, with al-Ghazali on love of God and the Ash'ari–Ibn Taymiyya debate over divine purposes

question: offspring-family
lede: Marriage is a divine sign of tranquillity and love and the way of the prophets; children are blessing and test, and parents are honoured next to God.
scope: The Qur'an and sound hadith on marriage, children and parents, with al-Ghazali's weighing of marriage; family law outside scope

question: love-beauty-creativity
lede: God is the Most Loving and loves beauty; human love and delight in beauty reflect Him, and al-Ghazali makes every true love finally love of God.
scope: The Qur'an and sound hadith on love and beauty, with al-Ghazali's account of love and music; the legal status of music and images left open

question: worship
lede: Humans were created to worship God alone; since a willing being always loves something as its god, the choice is between worship of the One and shirk.
scope: The Qur'an and sound hadith on 'ibada and shirk, with Ibn Taymiyya on the fitra and al-Ghazali on love

question: great-and-terrible
lede: One created nature, honoured by God and born on the fitra, holds both a longing to know and a craving to dominate; evil is that created power misdirected, and each soul answers for its own deeds.
scope: Mainstream Sunni thought, led by al-Ghazali, with Ash'ari, Maturidi and Ibn Taymiyya's positions

question: know-the-good
lede: God creates every person with a natural disposition (fitra) toward him and a soul inspired to know its own rebellion and piety; revelation guides both. The schools differ over how far reason knows good and evil without revelation.
scope: Qur’an and hadith on moral awareness, with limited Ash‘ari, Maturidi and Mu‘tazili distinctions

question: fail-the-good
lede: Moral awareness can be overridden by desire and habits that darken the heart; responsibility remains because recognizing the good does not prevent choosing against it.
scope: Qur'an and sound hadith, with al-Ghazali's Sunni moral psychology and a limited Ibn Taymiyya distinction

question: evil
lede: Nothing, good or ill, happens outside God's decree, yet the wrongdoer is truly answerable and blameworthy. Sunni theologians differ over how God's creating of acts and human responsibility fit together.
scope: Qur’anic good and ill (4:78–79), with differentiated Sunni theological accounts: al-Ash’ari, al-Maturidi, al-Razi’s commentary and Ibn Taymiyya
provenanceNotes: razi-mafatih-al-ghayb on 4:78, pp. 2–3; on 4:79, pp. 1–2: Arabic; paraphrased

question: suffering
lede: Suffering can be testing, consequence, or expiation under God’s decree; gratitude and patience express the believer’s response without revealing every affliction’s particular purpose.
scope: Qur’anic testing and decree, affliction hadith, and limited Sunni theodicy

question: death
lede: God appoints death within a life of testing and accountability; mortality is unavoidable and is not explained as punishment for inherited guilt.
scope: Qur’anic mortality, appointed term and accountability

question: self-deception
lede: A heart shaped by desire can call corruption reform and mistake misguided action for good, even while its bearer retains grounds for recognizing the truth.
scope: Qur’anic self-deception and al-Ghazali on the heart’s distorted judgment

question: self-salvation
lede: Weakness, sin and forgetfulness call for God’s guidance, faith and tawba; genuine effort and purification matter, but salvation ultimately depends on divine mercy.
scope: Classical Sunni diagnosis, repentance, guidance and mercy

question: guilt
lede: Tawba receives God’s mercy through sincere return, while forgiveness does not make victims’ rights or accountability disappear.
scope: Qur’anic repentance and Sunni hadith on victims’ rights

question: after-death
lede: Death is followed by a barrier until bodily resurrection and judgment; divine mercy and permitted intercession remain central to the final outcome.
scope: Qur’anic resurrection and judgment with Sunni reports on the grave and on intercession

question: final-end
lede: The final good includes enduring paradise, God’s good pleasure and, in Sunni teaching, seeing God; judgment and divine mercy qualify who attains it.
scope: Qur’anic paradise and Sunni vision of God

question: revelation
lede: Yes. The Qur'an is God's final revelation, sent down to Muhammad. Its matchless character, consistency and message, together with the Prophet's life and signs, show that it comes from God.
scope: Sunni account of revelation: the Qur'an as sent down to Muhammad, its challenge of inimitability (iʿjāz, with al-Baqillani's three aspects), consistency and confirmation of earlier scripture (with the doctrine of taḥrīf), and al-Ghazali's converging-evidence account of how a prophet is known; the Twelver Shi'a view of the Imams and the received Qur'an noted; textual preservation treated separately from inspiration

question: history
lede: History is a single line of sacred history, from creation through God's messengers to Muhammad, ending in the Hour of resurrection and judgement. Within it, peoples rise and fall under God's moral law.
scope: Qur'anic sacred history from creation through the succession of messengers to Muhammad and the Hour of resurrection and judgement; the rise and fall of peoples as moral lessons; Ibn Khaldun's dynastic cycles read within that linear frame; hadith on Jesus' return; Sunni expectations of the Mahdi and the Twelver doctrine of the hidden twelfth Imam

question: jesus
lede: Jesus is the Messiah and a uniquely honoured prophet born of Mary, but not God or God's Son. The standard Muslim reading holds that his enemies did not kill or crucify him, and that God raised him to himself.
scope: The Qur'anic Jesus (3:45–59, 4:157–159, 4:171, 5:72–75, 19:30–34, 61:6) and the classical exegesis of 4:157 in al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir; the classical doctrine of taḥrīf (Qur'an 2:75–79, 3:78, 5:13–15, 5:43–48, 10:94; Ibn Taymiyya's al-Jawāb al-ṣaḥīḥ; Ibn Ḥajar on the report from Ibn ʿAbbas); modern Muslim readings (Fatoohi); and a historical comparison with the first-century evidence for the crucifixion

question: ultimate-reality
lede: Hindu Vedānta traditions locate ultimate reality in Brahman, the source, support and end of all things, but disagree about whether the world and individual selves are finally distinct from Brahman.
scope: The Upaniṣads and Brahma Sūtra read through the three classical Vedānta schools: Advaita (Śaṅkara), Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) and Dvaita (Madhva)

question: something-rather-than-nothing
lede: Most Hindu traditions do not ask how something began from nothing. Being has always been: the world flows from Brahman and returns to it in beginningless cycles, and the Lord creates not from need but as play.
scope: The Ṛgveda and Upaniṣads, the Vedānta commentators on Brahma Sūtra II.1.33–34, and the Nyāya argument of Udayana

question: ultimate-personal
lede: In theistic Vedānta, yes: for Rāmānuja and Madhva the supreme reality is a personal Lord. Advaita treats the personal Lord as real at the level of worship and ordinary experience, but the highest Brahman as beyond all qualities.
scope: The Upaniṣads' personal and apophatic language, read through Advaita (Śaṅkara), Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) and Dvaita (Madhva)

question: order
lede: Hindu traditions root the world's order in Brahman: a cosmic order (ṛta), the Lord's inner rule and the moral law of karma hold it together. It is a moral as well as a natural order, not simply laws of physics.
scope: Vedic ṛta, the Upaniṣadic inner ruler and karma, the Vedānta commentators on order (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva), and Nyāya's inference to a maker

question: one-and-many
lede: All Vedānta schools trace the many to one Brahman, but differ on what the many are: names and forms of Brahman (Advaita), Brahman's real body (Rāmānuja), or realities eternally distinct from God (Madhva).
scope: Shared Upaniṣadic texts on the one and the many, read by Advaita (Śaṅkara), Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) and Dvaita (Madhva)

question: knowledge-possible
lede: Reliable means of knowledge, chiefly perception, inference and trustworthy testimony, put the knower in touch with the world and correct their own errors. Advaita adds that this holds only short of final knowledge of Brahman.
scope: The pramana theory of the Nyaya and Mimamsa schools, Advaita Vedanta's two levels of knowledge (Shankara), and the realist Vedanta of Ramanuja and Madhva

question: logic-binding
lede: Reasoning binds because a good inference tracks a real connection in the world, such as the invariable link between smoke and fire. Indian schools study logic as the account of how inference yields knowledge.
scope: Logic as the theory of knowledge-yielding inference in the Nyaya school (the five-membered argument, pervasion, suppositional reasoning), with Mimamsa and Advaita positions noted; SEP used as the school map

question: induction
lede: Inference reaches the unseen because some connections, like smoke and fire, hold without exception, and careful observation checked for hidden conditions can establish them. Materialist critics denied that this can ever be known.
scope: The Indian debate over knowing pervasion (vyapti): the Carvaka critique as reported in Madhava's Sarvadarsanasamgraha, and the Nyaya response by observation, the search for hidden conditions and suppositional reasoning, mapped by SEP

question: ultimate-authority
lede: For matters beyond ordinary perception, especially dharma and Brahman, the major orthodox traditions give final authority to śruti, the revealed Veda, though they disagree sharply over why it is authoritative and what it means.
scope: Scriptural authority (śruti) in the orthodox schools: Mimamsa's authorless Veda (Kumarila), Nyaya's reliable authors, and the three Vedanta commentators Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva on scripture, reason and realization

question: what-is-man
lede: A human being is an eternal conscious self embodied in a changing body-mind and reborn under karma. For Advaita that Self is one consciousness in all bodies; for Rāmānuja and Madhva souls are many, real and dependent on God.
scope: The Upaniṣads and Bhagavad Gītā read through Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita Vedānta

question: why-alive
lede: The rare human birth is for life's legitimate aims and, beyond them, liberation, which Advaita understands as knowing the Self to be Brahman and Rāmānuja as the soul's dependent enjoyment of God.
scope: The Gītā and dharmaśāstra on life's aims, read through Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta

question: offspring-family
lede: Household life is a sacred stage of dharma that supports all others and repays debts to the ancestors, within a path that culminates in renunciation.
scope: Upaniṣads, Gītā and the Manusmṛti on household life and its stages; Manu's authority and gender provisions disclosed

question: love-beauty-creativity
lede: Love is above all bhakti, which Rāmānuja says the Lord himself awakens; glory springs from the divine splendour, and Brahman is bliss.
scope: Upaniṣads and the Gītā read through Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita; classical aesthetic theory not treated

question: worship
lede: In the Gītā, worship is loving offering to the Lord, from a leaf or a flower to every act of life. Rāmānuja treats such devotion as the soul's highest relation to God; Advaita values it as preparation for liberating knowledge.
scope: The Bhagavad Gītā on devotion and contemplation, read through Śaṅkara and Rāmānuja; temple worship described only generally

question: great-and-terrible
lede: Humans are great because each is a conscious self that longs for the immortal, and terrible because desire, karma and ignorance obscure that self. The schools differ over the self's relation to God and whether all souls share one destiny.
scope: The Bhagavad Gītā read through Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita Vedānta

question: know-the-good
lede: The good is dharma, known above all from scripture, received tradition and the conduct of the wise. Discerning it means choosing the good over the merely pleasant rather than following desire.
scope: Gita, Katha Upanishad and Manu on dharma, with Mimamsa’s injunction-based account

question: fail-the-good
lede: The Gītā's answer is desire: born of restless passion, it veils knowledge through the senses, mind and understanding and turns to anger when frustrated, so a person can see the right and still be driven against it.
scope: The Bhagavad Gita, with Shankara and Ramanuja on desire, knowledge and agency

question: evil
lede: Evil comes from desire, anger and greed and from an intellect that takes wrong for right. Beneath them lies ignorance, which Advaita traces to confusing the Self with body and mind, and Rāmānuja to karma obscuring a real soul's knowledge.
scope: Gītā moral disorder and differentiated Vedānta/Nyāya explanations

question: suffering
lede: Suffering belongs to embodied, changing existence and to the fruits of past deeds, which Vedānta says the Lord dispenses justly rather than arbitrarily. Advaita adds that its root is the Self's mistaken identification with body and mind.
scope: Gita endurance, Yoga affliction, and Vedanta accounts of karma and selfhood

question: death
lede: The body dies but the self does not: it passes to another body as desire and action have shaped it. Death therefore belongs to the round of bondage, and the hope is release from rebirth, not mere survival.
scope: Gītā and Upaniṣadic mortality, with Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita distinctions

question: self-deception
lede: In the Gītā, desire veils understanding and a darkened intellect can take wrong for right, so a person keeps some knowledge while attachment steers its use. Advaita adds a deeper confusion of the Self with body and mind.
scope: The Gita’s corrupted discernment, with Shankara’s superimposition and Ramanuja’s contrasting selfhood

question: self-salvation
lede: The human problem is bondage to rebirth through desire, ignorance and karma. The remedy is liberation, reached in Advaita through knowledge of the Self and in theistic Vedānta through devotion, refuge and the Lord's grace.
scope: The Gītā through Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita Vedānta

question: guilt
lede: Wrongdoing binds the self through karma. For Advaita, liberating knowledge removes karma's power to bind; for Rāmānuja, the Lord, approached in knowledge and devotion, removes sin and his own displeasure.
scope: Gītā and Vedānta differences concerning sin and karmic bondage

question: after-death
lede: At death the self takes another body as its desires and deeds have conditioned it. Liberation ends rebirth: as nondual realization in Advaita, or as the soul's lasting, dependent bliss with the Lord in theistic Vedānta.
scope: Upaniṣadic rebirth and three Vedānta accounts of liberation

question: final-end
lede: The final end is liberation (moksha) from rebirth: for Advaita, realizing that the Self is nondual; for Rāmānuja and Madhva, the liberated soul's lasting, dependent bliss with the Lord.
scope: Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita final liberation

question: revelation
lede: Hindu traditions regard the Veda as śruti, an eternal disclosure of truths ordinary perception cannot reach, found by ancient seers rather than composed. The schools disagree about why it is authoritative.
scope: Revelation in the orthodox Hindu schools: the Veda as eternal śruti found by the seers, smṛti and divine descent (avatāra), with Śaṅkara and Rāmānuja on scripture and incarnation, and Vedic scholarship on composition and oral transmission for historical evaluation

question: history
lede: Cosmic history repeats through vast cycles of creation, decline, dissolution and renewal. God descends in every age to restore dharma, but the cycles reach no final goal; liberation means escaping them.
scope: Hindu cosmic time in the Bhagavad Gita, the Laws of Manu and the Vishnu Purana: kalpas and yugas, the decline and restoration of dharma, Vishnu's descents and Kalki, and liberation from the cycles, with Shankara's commentary and the Vaishnava account of divine governance

question: jesus
lede: Classical Hindu texts say nothing about Jesus. Modern Hindu thinkers have honoured him in different ways, as a moral teacher, a divine teacher or one incarnation among many, while rejecting the claim that he is God's only Son.
scope: Modern Hindu receptions of Jesus, presented as receptions rather than classical doctrine: Rammohun Roy's Unitarian reading, Vivekananda's Jesus as one incarnation among many, and Gandhi's divine teacher and martyr; compared with the avatara doctrine of the Gita and with the earliest historical evidence

question: ultimate-reality
lede: Buddhism places no permanent being or substance beneath reality. Conditioned things arise from causes and pass away, and liberation is freedom from that conditioned process, not union with a hidden ground.
scope: The Pāli discourses with Theravāda systematization (Buddhaghosa), and Mahāyāna Madhyamaka (Nāgārjuna) and Yogācāra (Vasubandhu) as the principal later analyses

question: something-rather-than-nothing
lede: Buddhism generally rejects the demand for a first beginning. The round of rebirth has no known start, and things arise from conditions, not from a creator and not from nothing.
scope: The Pāli discourses on beginnings and creators, Buddhaghosa, and Vasubandhu's Abhidharma argument against a creator God

question: ultimate-personal
lede: Buddhism has no personal creator or personal ground of reality. Buddhas and bodhisattvas are persons revered with deep devotion, but nirvāṇa and emptiness are neither persons nor impersonal gods.
scope: The Pāli discourses on Brahmā and the unconditioned, Theravāda analysis of persons, and Mahāyāna Buddha-nature and Pure Land devotion

question: order
lede: Reality is orderly because things arise from conditions in a constant, reliable pattern. That pattern holds whether or not anyone discovers it, and no lawgiver stands behind it.
scope: Dependent origination in the Pāli discourses, karma as part of conditional order, Vasubandhu's rejection of a divine orderer, and Madhyamaka on emptiness and conditionality

question: one-and-many
lede: Neither unity nor plurality is ultimate. Things are many because they arise from many conditions, and connected because each depends on others, but nothing, not even emptiness, is a hidden One beneath them.
scope: The Pāli middle way, Theravāda analysis of wholes, Madhyamaka emptiness, and Tiantai as one East Asian example

question: knowledge-possible
lede: Buddhism treats knowledge as tested cognition: perception and inference can be reliable when checked against experience, and liberating truth is ultimately to be directly realized.
scope: The Pali discourses on tested faith and direct knowledge; Dharmakirti's theory of perception and inference; Madhyamaka (Nagarjuna) and Yogacara (Vasubandhu) as later critiques
provenanceNotes: dharmakirti-pv-gretil PV II.1: Sanskrit; our paraphrase

question: logic-binding
lede: A sound inference binds because it rests on real relations between things: identity of nature, or cause and effect. Buddhism built a sophisticated logic on this, though some schools deny logic any ultimate foundation.
scope: Dharmakirti's theory of good reasons and necessary connection (Nyayabindu, with SEP as map); Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka use of reductio; the Pali canon's cautions about reasoning

question: induction
lede: Buddhist logicians held that inference reaches unobserved cases when it rests on real relations of identity or cause and effect, which are discovered through experience. Whether this escapes the problem of induction is still disputed.
scope: Dharmakirti's account of inference grounded in identity and causation (Nyayabindu; SEP as map), the canonical teaching that conditionality holds whether Buddhas arise or not, and the scholarly dispute (Gillon, Tillemans) over whether an induction problem remains

question: ultimate-authority
lede: The Dhamma is the final standard, but its truth is meant to be tested and directly realized rather than accepted merely because a teacher said it.
scope: The Pali discourses on the Dhamma as refuge and teacher (DN 16, AN 4.180, AN 3.65, MN 95), and Dharmakirti on the Buddha and scripture as means of knowledge; Mahayana sutra authority is deferred to Revelation & History
provenanceNotes: dharmakirti-pv-gretil PV II.7–10: Sanskrit; our paraphrase
dharmakirti-pv-gretil PV II.1, II.5: Sanskrit; our paraphrase
dharmakirti-pv-gretil PV II.7–10: Sanskrit; our paraphrase

question: what-is-man
lede: A human being is a process of five aggregates, none of them a self, yet a real conventional agent; human birth is prized as the rare chance to awaken.
scope: Early Buddhism and Theravāda as baseline, with Abhidharma, Yogācāra, Madhyamaka and buddha-nature distinctions

question: why-alive
lede: No creator assigns life a purpose; the rare human birth is the chance for the noble quest of awakening, which Mahāyāna pursues for all beings.
scope: Early Buddhist discourses as baseline, with Mahāyāna bodhisattva aspiration as a material difference

question: offspring-family
lede: Lay family life has a full ethic of reciprocal duties, with parents revered like gods; but there is no command to procreate, and going forth is higher.
scope: Pāli discourses on lay household ethics and monastic renunciation; later East Asian practice not surveyed

question: love-beauty-creativity
lede: Love at its best is boundless goodwill, not attachment; beauty is real but impermanent, and arts serve devotion while monastics renounce shows.
scope: Pāli discourses on love, beauty and the arts, with Buddhaghosa; later Buddhist art traditions not surveyed

question: worship
lede: Buddhism worships no creator, yet treats reverence as a human need: the Buddha honours the Dhamma, practice is the highest honour, and devotion takes many forms.
scope: Pāli discourses on reverence, refuge and honour, with Pure Land devotion as a distinct form; no creator-worship implied

question: great-and-terrible
lede: Buddhist traditions explain goodness and cruelty through conditioned mental states: greed, hatred and delusion yield harmful action, their opposites yield wholesome action, and these defilements can be uprooted.
scope: Early Buddhism and Theravāda, Abhidharma and Yogācāra, Madhyamaka, Buddha-nature traditions and Zen

question: know-the-good
lede: Actions rooted in greed, hatred and delusion are unwholesome, and those free of them wholesome. Their harm or benefit to oneself and others shows the difference, and reflection, wise counsel and practice train judgment.
scope: Early Buddhist discernment, the Kalama discourse in context, and Theravada conscience

question: fail-the-good
lede: Understanding that greed, aversion, and delusion are harmful does not uproot their conditioned tendencies; they can still govern action until deeper cultivation changes the mind.
scope: Early Buddhist discourses on unwholesome roots and persistent tendencies, with Theravada clarification from Buddhaghosa

question: evil
lede: Evil is unwholesome intention and action, such as killing, stealing and lying, rooted in greed, hatred and delusion, and harmful to oneself and others; the schools differ over how such defilement relates to ultimate reality.
scope: Early Buddhist roots and agency, with Madhyamaka, Zen and Tiantai contrasts

question: suffering
lede: Suffering involves bodily pain and the wider instability of clinging existence; craving, aversion, and ignorance add distress which the path seeks to end.
scope: Four Noble Truths, dependent origination and the two arrows, with Theravada and Mahayana clarification

question: death
lede: Death arises with birth in conditioned existence; mindful recollection should produce diligence, while the answer to mortality is not an immortal self.
scope: Early Buddhist and Theravāda mortality, with Śāntideva on urgency

question: self-deception
lede: Ignorance and craving can distort perception and sustain a mistaken self-view beneath deliberate judgment; possessing correct information does not uproot those tendencies.
scope: Early Buddhist distortions, Theravada ignorance, and a limited Yogacara contrast

question: self-salvation
lede: Suffering (dukkha) arises from craving and ignorance and ends through the Eightfold Path of ethics, meditation and wisdom. Pure Land relies on Amida Buddha's vow, the Other Power Shinran stresses for those who cannot free themselves.
scope: Nikāya/Theravāda baseline with Mahāyāna and Pure Land distinctions

question: guilt
lede: Wrongdoing calls for honest recognition, disclosure to a teacher or companion, restraint, and cultivation that can weaken its karmic results. One Pure Land sutra adds Amitābha's help at death even for grave offenders.
scope: Nikāya moral repair with a bounded Pure Land comparison

question: after-death
lede: Ordinary rebirth is conditioned continuity without a migrating self; the liberated one’s fate resists simple survival or annihilation descriptions.
scope: Nikāya rebirth and final release with a bounded Pure Land contrast

question: final-end
lede: The final good is release from craving and ignorance; Mahāyāna foregrounds awakening for others, and Pure Land birth serves Buddhahood rather than an eternal ego.
scope: Nikāya nirvana, bodhisattva aspiration and a Pure Land contrast

question: revelation
lede: Buddhism does not teach revelation from a creator. The Buddha claims to have discovered a timeless path, and his teaching is recognized by its agreement with the Dhamma and confirmed by realization in practice.
scope: Buddhist disclosure rather than creator revelation: the Buddha as discoverer of an ancient path (SN 12.65), tests of Buddha-word in the Pali discourses, and the Mahayana case for later sutras (Lotus Sutra II and XV; Shantideva, Bodhicaryavatara 9.42–44), with scholarship on oral transmission and canonical chronology

question: history
lede: Saṃsāra has no known beginning, and world-systems arise and pass away over immense ages. Buddhas and their teaching appear and decline within these cycles, and liberation escapes the process rather than completing it.
scope: Early Buddhist teaching on time and history in the Pali discourses: beginningless transmigration (SN 15), cosmic contraction, expansion and destruction (DN 27, AN 7.66), moral decline and recovery with the coming Buddha Metteyya (DN 26), and the decline of the teaching (SN 16.13, AN 8.51)

question: jesus
lede: Buddhist canonical texts say nothing about Jesus. Modern Buddhist teachers often honour him as a great spiritual teacher, even an enlightened being, while rejecting the Christian beliefs in a Creator, incarnation and resurrection.
scope: Modern Buddhist receptions of Jesus, presented as receptions rather than canonical doctrine: Soyen Shaku's Dharmakaya reading and the Dalai Lama's 'enlightened being or bodhisattva' (as quoted by Cobb), with the Buddhist reasons for rejecting creator, incarnation and resurrection, and Shinran's Pure Land as the closest analogue to salvation by another
provenanceNotes: cobb-review-good-heart p. 580: the Dalai Lama, as quoted by Cobb
